decisions.title: The gate's test leg runs every test binary; it never stops at the first failure
decisions.decided_by: The gate test-leg card's words and its lead's answers; recorded with LYSGATE-001
decisions.context: The gate's test leg runs cargo test over the workspace with all features and without --no-fail-fast, so it stops at the first failing test binary: a run that fails in one crate reports nothing about the binaries and crates after it, and a gate can go red for one reason while hiding others. project.json's legs are copied verbatim into every new cluster's gate, so the fail-fast form spreads with each cluster.
decisions.decision: Every declaration of the gate's test leg runs `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast`: project.json, every cluster design.json gate, .land/gates.sh and CLAUDE.md's 'Gates before any commit' block; CI's test step gains the same one flag and nothing else. Rejected: keeping cargo's default fail-fast run, which is shorter on a red round but reports only the first failing binary.
consequences: A new cluster's gate copied from project.json carries --no-fail-fast.
A red test leg runs every test binary before it exits, so a red round holds the build venue's battery lock longer than a fail-fast run did.
The leg still exits non-zero when any test fails; no timeout is raised and no test is split to compensate.
--no-fail-fast does not continue past a compile error, so evidence that every binary ran comes from a planted test that compiles and fails.

decisions.title: The Claude Code render refuses by name what it cannot shape and never writes a default in place of a value the record did not carry
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings and answers to the render-refusal survey; recorded with HOME-008
decisions.context: The Claude Code render filled in a default wherever a home record was missing a field or carried one of the wrong type (an empty role, tool_use_id, text, name or model, an empty content array or input object, is_error false, end_turn for any stopReason, a null signature) and serialised its loss account and the hashes of dropped parts with unwrap_or_default, so a broken session rendered to a file that looked whole and the render reported success.
decisions.decision: Every value the render copies from a message entry must be present and of the type the target field takes; a missing field or a field of another type refuses the render by the session, the entry id, the field and the expected type, and nothing is written. The value itself is never named, except an unmapped stopReason, which is named because it is a protocol value and not transcript. Every serialisation the render needs, the records, the dropped parts it hashes and the loss account, is done before any directory or file is created, and a failure refuses by name. Only three values are written that the record does not carry, and they are format constants Claude Code's file requires on every record: gitBranch "", usage {input_tokens 0, output_tokens 0} and stop_sequence null. Only one field reads a meaning from its absence: a thinking part with no `redacted` field is not redacted, since in Pi's grammar the field is optional and its absence is the source's own statement; a `redacted` present and not a boolean refuses. stopReason is mapped by one explicit arm per value Pi's grammar carries: toolUse to tool_use, length to max_tokens, stop to end_turn, error to stop_sequence (the value Claude Code writes on its own errored turns, measured), and aborted, for which Claude Code writes no value of its own, refuses by name, as does any other value. A present role the render does not know is still skipped. render-launch stores its template in the home only after the render has succeeded. Rejected: rendering a default and naming it in the loss account, refusing only missing fields and copying wrongly typed ones, mapping every unknown stopReason to end_turn, and keeping the template a refused launch had already stored.
consequences: resolve_given lists appended_instructions and mcp_config ahead of user_claude_md, and the lys.given data shape of ADR-013 is unchanged.

RECORD.md states the one rule and names the old order as superseded by the commit that lands HOME-011 and its date; a reader tells an entry's order by comparing its recorded time with that date, and never by its harness_version.
A later harness card records its documents in the order its harness's request gives, and a harness-side input the request carries no trace of takes its place from the read order until it is measured.
A card that measures a real MCP server's tools position fixes mcp_config's place by that measurement.
A session, canon or fork child holding an entry the render cannot shape no longer renders; the refusal names the entry to repair and nothing is written.

Sessions the importer wrote with a redacted_thinking part that carried no data hold thinkingSignature null and now refuse to render; the importer's own defaults are the other half of the defect and belong to the importer card, not to the render.
A session holding an aborted turn does not render until the Claude Code format has a value for it.
The bytes rendered from a session that carries every field do not change, so every pinned render hash stands.

decisions.title: A home moves as one fast-forward git ref pushed to a path on this machine, tracking exactly its record stores
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the move survey; recorded with HOME-019
decisions.context: Stage 3 of the context roadmap moves a home by a pushed ref the target fetches, never a hand copy, with encryption before any bytes leave the machine as its precondition. A home holds, beside its record, lock files and temporaries that must never travel; its blocks hold imported tool results verbatim and a template's env and mcp slots are free strings, so no scan can promise a home holds no secret; and git's own settings can change bytes on the way in or out.
decisions.decision: A home directory is a git repository whose tracked files are exactly each session's file, index and head, each block and each template, enumerated by name and never by pattern; the first ship initialises it. ship holds every session's lock through its check and snapshot, commits that set, and pushes it without force as the one ref refs/lys/home to a bare repository at a path on this machine, creating it when the path does not exist; a remote ref the new commit does not descend from is refused as ref_diverged. Every other remote, ssh to any host, https, git or file URLs and hosted services, is refused as remote_not_local until stage 3's encryption exists. git runs as the binary with a pinned environment and no filters. Rejected: an allow-list of estate ssh hosts, scanning the home for secrets, a pure-Rust git crate, and force-pushing or overwriting a ref.
consequences: No byte of a home leaves this machine through ship until the secrets step's encryption lands; the second-machine block fetches this ref after that.

A home with no session, a stale or missing index or head, a session a live owner holds, a repository tracking other files and a remote path that is not a bare repository are each refused by name before anything is pushed.
The gate machine needs git on PATH.

decisions.title: An arrival is a seventh lys.harness_event kind, one per arriving session, hung beside the head
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the move survey, and the lead's answer that fetch commits the arrival; recorded with HOME-019
decisions.context: Stage 3 gives the target a distinct execution id with its ancestry recorded, and the identity documents describe an execution per session or fork. The source is never written, so the ancestry can only be written on the target side, and the arrival is a fact about the record, not a turn.
decisions.decision: fetch appends to each arriving session one lys.harness_event of kind arrival whose detail carries the source commit, the remote, the ref and a fresh execution id for that session's continuation. It hangs beside the head through append_beside, as template_render does (ADR-012), so the head file, the head hash and the next render's session_head on the target are the source's. fetch then commits the appended entries as one commit whose parent is the fetched commit, naming the source commit, the remote and the ref, so the target's git status is clean and a later ship from it carries the arrival onward; a failed append or commit removes what fetch created. There is no home-level id file and no block is stored for it. Rejected: an arrival that moves the head, arrival lines left uncommitted until the target's next ship, one execution id per home, and a block for the arrival's data.
consequences: A target's head file is byte-identical to the source's after fetch, and a render of the target records the source's session_head.
A remote whose arrival data would pass the 512-byte cap is refused before fetch writes anything.
The target's HEAD is one arrival commit on the fetched commit, and a ship from the target carries the arrival to the next home.

decisions.title: A home moves as one pushed git ref of an allowlisted tracked set, never a hand copy
decisions.context: Stage 3 of the context roadmap moves a home off the machine that captured it, by the route a build tree takes: a pushed ref the target fetches. A home holds session files, their index, head and lock files, the block store and the template store, and blocks hold raw request and response bodies. Copying the directory by hand carries lock and temporary files, has no commit to name what moved, and leaves no ancestry; tracking the whole directory carries whatever else lands in it. The shape is decided before stage 3's second block fetches it from another machine (docs/design/home/briefs/HOME-004.json).
decisions.decision: A home is a git repository whose tracked set is an allowlist: sessions/<id>.jsonl, <id>.index.jsonl and <id>.head, the files under blocks/ and the files under templates/, never a lock, temporary, environment, render or execution-id file. `lys-home ship` commits exactly that set with git run apart from the person's configuration and pushes it without force as one ref, refs/lys-home/<commit>, to a remote named on the command line; `lys-home fetch` fetches that ref into a new home. Rejected: a hand copy or an archive of the directory, which names no commit and records no ancestry; tracking the whole directory, which ships whatever else is in it; and a pure-Rust git crate, which adds a dependency where the git binary suffices. Until encryption at rest exists, ship refuses a remote off this machine and any tracked file holding a value of the named secret values file or matching one of five standard secret patterns (private key header, sk- token, GitHub token, AWS access key id, JWT).
consequences: RECORD.md names the tracked set, the ref namespace and the home's own branch refs/heads/lys-home.
Ship and fetch check an index and a head without rebuilding either, so a source home is never written outside .git/ and a target refuses rather than repairs.
Stage 3's second block fetches this ref from another machine, and the off-machine refusal is lifted by the encryption-at-rest card, not before.
A later change to the tracked set is a decision alongside this one, since a fetched home depends on what was shipped.

decisions.title: An arrival is a seventh lys.harness_event kind, hung beside the head and written by fetch
decisions.context: A fetched home must record where it came from and carry its own execution id, so that its ancestry is on the record. The lys.harness_event kinds are a closed set of six, and ADR-012 rejected advancing the head for a record the model never sees, because it moves the session head hash and splits renders of one session. This extends the closed kind set and adds execution identity to the home, so it is written down on its own (docs/design/home/briefs/HOME-004.json).
decisions.decision: Fetch appends to each session one lys.harness_event of kind `arrival`, with source_uuid and record null and a detail of exactly source_commit, remote, ref and execution_id, hung beside the head with append_beside so the head and the session head hash do not move; the execution id is one per target home, fresh at fetch, kept in the untracked file <home>/execution-id. The remote is recorded as a canonical path, a file:/// URL, or a URL without userinfo, and the data stays within the 512-byte cap. Rejected: appending the arrival on the context path, which moves the head (ADR-012); a new custom entry type, which adds a type where the harness event carries the same shape; and one execution id per session, where the words give the home one.
consequences: RECORD.md lists arrival among the lys.harness_event kinds with its four detail keys.
No importer maps a harness record to the arrival kind; only fetch writes it.
A render of a fetched home carries the same session head hash as a render of its source.
A remote that would push the arrival past the cap is refused at fetch before the target exists.

decisions.title: A translation to another harness is a per-target, per-version renderer of our own with a loss account, never that harness's importer
decisions.context: The home promises that a session can move to another harness, and translation had been designed and not proved. Codex already ships an importer of Claude Code files; measured in the lantern work (tools/lantern/docs/02-SESSION-FORMATS.md section 3), it is a compaction and not a copy: it drops thinking, sidechains and meta records, clips tool input and tool results, and records no account of what it dropped. The ruling recorded there was to improve on it and not adopt it. The first pair, Claude Code to Codex 0.156.0, is built in HOME-004, and every later pair (Codex to Claude Code, Pi) will face the same fork, so the shape is decided once.
decisions.decision: A translation to another harness is a renderer of our own, one per target harness and per measured version, over the home's context path: it carries every text part, tool call and tool result whole as the target's own items, carries readable thinking as text and drops opaque blocks by hash (home P3), announces itself in band as a translated context naming its source session and head hash, writes a JSON loss account beside its output listing kept, changed and lost by entry id and block hash, and is recorded on the session as a side leaf. It is not the target harness's own importer, adopted, wrapped or called, because that importer is a compaction that loses what the home keeps and cannot say what it lost; and it is not one renderer for every version, because a harness's file shape is a per-version measurement (home P6).
consequences: Each target version is measured from files that version wrote before it is rendered for; an unmeasured version is refused by name.
Every translation writes a loss account whose block hashes key to the home's block store.
Every translated thread carries an in-band marker naming its source session and head hash.
The target harness's importer is never a dependency and its code is never copied.
Later pairs (Codex to Claude Code, Pi) are their own renderers under this rule, each proved on its own.

decisions.title: Audit receipts are for changes only; answered permission checks go to step 2's separate access record
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W1); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: The audit receipt card asked whether a permission check that is merely answered, not changed, leaves a receipt. Every signed receipt is a leaf in the lys log in operation order (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.md:49); a check is answered many times a minute once step 2 enforces anything, so putting answered checks into the signed receipt log would make it a high-volume access log that drowns the changes it exists to prove.
decisions.decision: Receipts are for changes only. A check that is answered and changes nothing is not a receipt. When step 2 brings enforcement, allows and refusals go into a separate access record that step 2 defines: refusals are always recorded there, and whether allows are too is decided with step 2. Rejected: every answered check as a signed receipt in the lys log, and deferring the question to the build.
decisions.quote: Receipts are for changes only. A check that is answered and changes nothing is not a receipt.
consequences: DIRECTORY-007 writes this as a boundary and as constraint CN15 of the directory design, so nobody later puts high-volume checks into the signed receipt log.
Step 2's access record is a non-goal of DIRECTORY-007; the brief that brings enforcement defines it and decides whether allows are recorded.
In step 1 nothing answers a permission check (CN11), so the only receipts are the listed changes and the directory service's sign-ins and sign-in refusals.

decisions.title: The receipt verifier lives in the lys CLI, offline, needing only the log and the service's public key
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W2); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: The audit receipt card asked where the verifier lives: the lys CLI or the directory service. A verifier is what a party holding only the log and the key uses to check the directory's history without the operator's cooperation (story S7, DIRECTORY-003 R2's read-only verification path).
decisions.decision: The verifier lives in the lys CLI, as lys log verify receipt, offline, needing only the log directory and the service's public key. Changing the published lys binary for this is accepted; the release that carries it is a separate, deliberate act after docs/design/identity/IDENTITY-EVENTS.md's envelope version is ratified and recorded, never before, because publishing a crate that exposes a format freezes it (CLAUDE.md:78-80). Rejected: a verifier inside the directory service, which would be checking the service with the service and defeats the point of an independent audit.
decisions.quote: A verifier that needs the running directory service would be checking the service with the service, which defeats the point of an independent audit.
consequences: DIRECTORY-007 R3 adds the subcommand under the published discipline of lys log verify: one refusal class for every cryptographic or structural failure, pre-crypto refusals named on their own.
The verifier's row lands on main behind a check that the ratified envelope version is on main; landing on main publishes nothing.
The receipt's signed encoding stays with IDENTITY-EVENTS.md under DIRECTORY-003's joint review; the verifier is written against that document's version field and freezes no wire format.

decisions.title: A development install emits test receipts under a test key and a test tag, and a real key never verifies one
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W3); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: Emitting any receipt outside a test is one of the three acts reserved for Tom (docs/design/lys-anchor/DECISIONS.md:333-335). A development install signs outside a cargo test harness, so its receipts had to be read either as that reserved act or as test receipts; read as the act, the whole path could never be proved end to end before Tom's release.
decisions.decision: A development install emits test receipts, signed with a test key and carrying a test tag, inside IDENTITY-001's development isolation, and never performs the reserved act. The verifier refuses a test-tagged receipt by name unless it is given the test key explicitly, and a real key never verifies a test receipt, so a test receipt never passes as real. Harness tests stay as well. Rejected: a development install that emits no receipts, and reading its receipts as the reserved act.
decisions.quote: A development install emits test receipts, signed with a test key and carrying a test tag, inside IDENTITY-001's development isolation, and never performs the act DECISIONS.md:335 reserves for Tom.
consequences: The test tag is the one field added to IDENTITY-001's receipt contract, under this ruling; IDENTITY-EVENTS.md carries it in the envelope.

lys log verify receipt takes --test-key beside --verifier-key: a test-tagged receipt is verified only against the test key and refused pre-crypto without it, saying to supply the test key; an untagged receipt is verified only against the verifier key.

DIRECTORY-007 R5 proves the whole path on the development install with test receipts and records the three outcomes: verified as a test receipt, refused for want of the test key, refused under another key.

decisions.title: An identity's lifecycle state is folded from its signed transition records and never set directly
decisions.decided_by: The lifecycle card's words, requested by tom; recorded with DIRECTORY-009
decisions.context: ADR-011 makes register, activate, suspend, reinstate and retire the only transitions, each one signed audit record, and DIRECTORY-003 R5 records the state beside each identity with its projection equal to replay. Nothing on main said whether the state is a value an API, a migration or a repair may write, which would leave two sources of truth: the stored state and the records that should explain it (principle P4 forbids a change followed by a best-effort log).
decisions.decision: The state at any moment is the fold of the identity's transition records in log order, from registered. No API, migration or repair sets a state; a transition validates against the folded state and the cause rule, appends its record through the directory's event path, and the state is read again by folding. A read answers the fold or refuses by name at the coordinate of a record the transition table refuses, and never answers a state past it, repairs the log or skips the record. Rejected: a stored state column set at transition and audited after it; a repair path that writes a state; and treating provisioned as a fifth state rather than a view over the facts beside the state.
decisions.quote: the state at any moment is folded from the log and never set directly
consequences: DIRECTORY-009 R3 builds the fold with a state type of exactly four values, and the state field DIRECTORY-003 R5's projection keeps is filled from the fold and from nothing else.

Retirement closes the identity and never its record: a retired identity's state, transitions and the record that put it there are read exactly as a live one's, and no row deletes or hides a record (L2, CN21).
A record the table refuses is a refusal named at its coordinate, answered by verifying the leaf against its receipt and reading the log by hand; the log is never repaired.
Every check that reads state reads the fold, so a suspended or retired identity fails by state alone whatever grants it holds.

decisions.title: A suspension takes effect at the next check, a session refresh is a check, and no Rauthy session is revoked at once
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answer L1 to the lifecycle card, from the lifecycle document on main; recorded with DIRECTORY-009
decisions.context: The lifecycle card asked whether a Rauthy session that outlives a suspension is revoked at once or at its next refresh. The lifecycle document says suspend and revoke both take effect at the next check and neither promises to roll back an action already admitted, and that a suspended identity's running executions stop at their next admission (docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:51-53 and docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:23); the directory design keeps open whether suspending a person also ends their sign-in session at Rauthy (its non-goals).
decisions.decision: A suspension or retirement takes effect at the next check and not before. The directory's resolution of a Rauthy-authenticated session at sign-in and at refresh is a check, so a session that outlives a suspension is refused at its next refresh and at every access check before that, by state, whatever grants it holds. Nothing in DIRECTORY-009 calls Rauthy to revoke, end or invalidate a session, keeps a list of sessions to end, or rolls back an admitted action. An at-once revocation of the Rauthy session would be a later revision of the suspend transition, and whether suspending also ends the sign-in session at Rauthy stays open as the design records it. Rejected: revoking the session at Rauthy at once within this brief, and treating a refresh as something other than a check.
decisions.quote: A refresh is a check, so a Rauthy session that outlives the suspension is refused at its next refresh and at every access check before that, by state, whatever grants it holds
consequences: DIRECTORY-009 R4 answers the access check state first and R5 refuses a suspended or retired identity at sign-in and at refresh by name, with the grant answerer called zero times.
The directory design gains constraint CN20 and a non-goal for the at-once revocation, so the later revision is a deliberate act and not a drift.
DIRECTORY-007 R4's step-1 leg that a suspended identity's sign-in is not refused on state is superseded when DIRECTORY-009 R5 lands, and the brief that lands second reconciles it under CN9.
An action admitted before a suspension stands; the record of the suspension is the only thing appended.

decisions.title: What a compaction could not keep is a lys.loss custom entry of ids, counts and SHA-256s
decisions.context: A Claude Code compaction replaces the model's context with a summary while the originals stay in the file. The home imports the compaction as Pi's compaction entry, which says where the kept range begins but never what fell outside it, so nothing in a home says what a compaction could not keep and nothing proves on a compacted session that the original is still there. Pi's grammar is adopted unchanged (P2), so any account has to be a lys custom entry, and a durable entry shape in the home is decided before homes carry it, as lys.given's was (ADR-013).
decisions.decision: Each compaction the importer writes is followed directly by one lys.loss custom entry, a side leaf whose parent is the compaction entry, whose data names the compaction by entry id, the first and last entry id of the span it summarised (the root-to-first-kept path entries, from the root or the previous compaction to the entry before the first kept one), the counts of that span's entries, messages, tool calls, tool results and blocks, its line bytes and block bytes counted separately, the counts of side-leaf and sidechain entries hanging from it by number only, the tokensBefore the harness reported (null when it reported none), a logicalParentUuid that names no record as unresolved, the SHA-256 of the span's first source line, of its last and of its lines concatenated in file order, the hash of the summary record's block and the span's distinct block hashes. Its keys are: compaction_id, first_kept (null when nothing is kept), span_first, span_last, entries, messages, tool_calls, tool_results, blocks, line_bytes, block_bytes, side_leaf_entries, sidechain_entries, tokens_before, unresolved_logical_parent, first_line_sha256, last_line_sha256, span_sha256, summary_record, block_hashes. Rejected: adding fields to Pi's compaction entry (it breaks CN4 and P2); hashing or listing side leaves and sidechain entries by id (their ids are drawn fresh on every import, so two imports of one file would disagree); and carrying any content, the summary included (P7).
consequences: HOME-010 adds the field to LanternData, the light act, its report and recall's rows, switches the fork to the typed field, and documents lit_in in docs/design/home/RECORD.md.
ADR-014's lantern shape is extended by one optional key, not replaced: a lantern lit before HOME-010 is read as it is and stays forkable.
ADR-017's older-record rule stays in force for a lantern with no lit_in; retiring it is a separate decision.

The fork's fixtures light with the light act every lantern it can produce, and write by hand only the records it cannot: a lantern with no lit_in, a copy whose lit_in names another session, and a malformed lit_in.
Once lanterns are lit under it in a real home the shape is frozen; a change to lit_in's meaning is a new version alongside.
RECORD.md states the rule, the exemption, the link-position rule and the unresolved marker.
Existing records are not rewritten; they compare by canonicalisation at check time.
A canonicalisation failure other than a path not existing is refused by path and operation.
The chain and the slug may see different forms of one working directory until the slug rule's own requirement settles it.
The loss entry is off the chain: context_path finds the compaction on the path unchanged and the render never writes the loss entry.
Two imports of one Claude Code file give loss entries equal byte for byte once the entry id, parentId, timestamp and data.compaction_id are masked.
The listing reads a span through the index and checks each named block by hash; a compaction with no loss entry, or pointing at itself, is reported unaccounted by entry id and never rewritten.
The shape is versioned by its custom type: a change is a new custom type alongside, never a mutation of lys.loss.

decisions.title: A Claude Code compaction imports as one Pi compaction at the summary record's place, keeping what Claude Code kept, and renders as the compact_boundary pair
decisions.decided_by: The home card lead's answers to the compaction survey; recorded with HOME-008
decisions.context: The importer handled only a legacy summary record, pointing the compaction at itself with tokensBefore 0; it read neither compact_boundary nor isCompactSummary, so a current compaction imported as a system harness event and a plain user message, and the render wrote a legacy summary line that the current Claude Code does not write. Measured on the survey's sample of 28 boundaries, anchorUuid named the summary record itself in 28 and all 94 preserved uuids sat before the boundary, so bounding the kept range by anchorUuid would count what Claude Code kept as lost and drop recent turns from the context path.
decisions.decision: A compact_boundary record imports as today, a lys.harness_event on the chain; the isCompactSummary record under it becomes one Pi compaction entry that takes that record's uuid, sits where the record sat as the child of the boundary's entry, carries the record's text as its summary and tokensBefore from compactMetadata.preTokens, and keeps the record only as a block; it is not a message entry. Its first kept entry is the earliest in file order of compactMetadata.preservedMessages.uuids when that list is non-empty, otherwise the first record whose parent is the summary record, and when there is none nothing is kept and firstKeptEntryId is the empty string, which keeps Pi's string type and is the only value that names no entry, so a compaction never names itself; anchorUuid is not used. A compact_boundary with no isCompactSummary record under it is not a compaction the harness completed: it stays a lys.harness_event, no summary is invented, and the listing reports it as a boundary without a summary. A legacy summary record keeps the entry its leafUuid names. A first kept entry not on record is refused by uuid. A logicalParentUuid naming no record is not refused. The Claude Code render writes a compaction as a compact_boundary record followed by an isCompactSummary user record holding the summary, then the kept entries, never the legacy summary line and never a custom entry. Rejected: bounding the kept range by anchorUuid; keeping the summary record as a message entry beside the compaction (the summary would be read twice); placing the compaction off the chain or re-parenting the next message (HOME-001 R3's parent-equals-source acceptance stands with no exception); and rendering the legacy summary line, which the current Claude Code does not write.
consequences: resolve_given lists appended_instructions and mcp_config ahead of user_claude_md, and the lys.given data shape of ADR-013 is unchanged.

RECORD.md states the one rule and names the old order as superseded by the commit that lands HOME-011 and its date; a reader tells an entry's order by comparing its recorded time with that date, and never by its harness_version.
A later harness card records its documents in the order its harness's request gives, and a harness-side input the request carries no trace of takes its place from the read order until it is measured.
A card that measures a real MCP server's tools position fixes mcp_config's place by that measurement.
HOME-001 R3's self-pointing summary mapping is replaced; the round-trip test that every message entry's parent equals its source parentUuid stands unchanged.
A home imported before this mapping is reported unaccounted by the listing; the act it names is re-importing the source file into a new home.

The rendered compact_boundary record's uuid is derived under render-uuid/v2, a new version alongside ADR-016's v1 that carries v1's derivation of the role record byte for byte and adds the role compact_boundary; v1's closed role list is not amended, a render with no compaction stays v1, and the render report names the version used.
The resume of the rendered pair is a per-version measurement (P6), recorded in PROOF-COMPACTION.md on Claude Code 2.1.283.
A boundary with no summary under it is counted by the listing by entry id, never turned into a compaction.

decisions.title: An admission policy judges at an instant its caller names; the live path names the present
decisions.decided_by: The card's words and the lys lead's answer on admit_at's parameters; recorded with LYSANCHOR-001
decisions.context: RecognisedCertificate could judge a certificate only at the present, because its admit called lys-core's verify_certificate_chain, which reads the clock itself. Its expiry test therefore slept 2.1 seconds, a wait the suite paid on every run and one whose outcome depends on a host's load. lys-core already exports verify_certificate_chain_at, frozen at 0.2.0, which takes the instant to judge against.
decisions.decision: RecognisedCertificate gains an inherent admit_at taking the submission, the SubmitterContext and the instant, built on verify_certificate_chain_at; AdmissionPolicy::admit keeps its signature and calls admit_at with the present, so a live request is judged exactly as before, and tests state the instants they judge at. Rejected: keeping the sleep; raising a timeout or splitting the test; injecting a clock into the policy instead of passing an instant; changing the AdmissionPolicy trait; and an admit_at taking only the asserted credential bytes, which would have to collapse the context's provenance before the call and could not represent the unidentified or transport-authenticated arms.
decisions.quote: The rule to meet: an admission policy judges at an instant its caller names.
consequences: The AdmissionPolicy trait, NotAdmitted and anchor/append.rs are unchanged; DP9 and DP23 in docs/design/lys-anchor/DECISIONS.md stand.
A test of the certificate gate's validity window states its instants and never sleeps.
lys-anchor depends on chrono through the workspace's existing entry.
verify_certificate_chain_at is used as lys-core 0.2.0 publishes it; lys-core is not changed.
